identify.title: Identify a cipher
identify.subtitle: Pasted a ciphertext you cannot name? The identification tool measures frequencies, periodicity and structure, then ranks the likely ciphers with its reasoning.

identify.title: Cipher identification
identify.subtitle: Paste a ciphertext and the tool measures what it can: letter frequencies, periodicity, structure. It then ranks the likely cipher families and concrete ciphers, and shows the reasoning behind every verdict.
identify.uploadTooLarge: That file is too large (100 KB max).
identify.tooShort: Too little text to analyse — at least 20 letters are needed.
identify.unreliable: Only {{letters}} letters to work with — treat the ranking below as a hint, not a verdict.

reasons.transpositionShape: The letter frequencies match English exactly (index of coincidence {{ic}}) — the letters were moved, not replaced.
reasons.transpositionNotEnglish: The letters as they stand are far from English, so they were replaced rather than moved — a transposition is unlikely.
reasons.substitutionShape: The frequency profile has the English shape, but the letters stand in the wrong places — a fixed substitution.
reasons.substitutionNotShuffled: The text already reads as English in its original letter order — no substitution was applied.
reasons.periodicPolyalphabetic: Reading every {{period}}-th letter gives English-like frequencies the text as a whole lacks — the signature of a periodic polyalphabetic cipher.
reasons.aperiodicPolyalphabetic: The index of coincidence ({{ic}}) is close to random and there is no periodic structure — a running-key or machine cipher.
reasons.polyalphabeticNotPeriodic: The index of coincidence is English-like and slices at every period look the same — no periodic polyalphabetic structure.
reasons.blockStructure: Even-length text with a reduced letter set — typical of digraph (two-letter) block ciphers.
reasons.blockOddLength: Odd text length rules out every digraph block cipher.
reasons.caesarBestShift: Shifting every letter back by {{shift}} makes the text read as English.
reasons.rot13Shift: The best shift is exactly 13 — the signature of ROT13.
reasons.atbashMirror: Reversing the alphabet (A↔Z, B↔Y, …) makes the text read as English.
reasons.affineKey: An affine key of {{key}} (multiply, then shift) makes the text read as English.
reasons.keywordNoSimpleKey: A substitution fits, but no shift, mirror or affine key does — the alphabet was likely rebuilt from a keyword.
reasons.vigenereSlices: Each slice of every {{period}}-th letter decrypts with a plain shift — the Vigenère signature.
reasons.albertiMixedDisc: The slices resist plain shifts — a mixed-alphabet disc, as on Alberti's cipher wheel.
reasons.enigmaAperiodic: Near-random letter frequencies with no periodic structure — characteristic of rotor machines like Enigma. Confidence stays low: ordinary noise looks similar.
reasons.railFenceUndo: Unravelling a {{rails}}-rail zigzag restores English letter pairs.
reasons.columnarWidth: Reading the text in columns of {{width}} restores English letter pairs.
reasons.playfairDigraphs: Even-length text with no doubled pair, no letter J and at most 25 letters — the rules of Playfair output.
reasons.playfairHasJ: The letter J appears — Playfair replaces it, so this cannot be Playfair.
reasons.adfgvxSet: The text uses only the letters {{letters}} — the ADFGVX fractionation alphabet.
reasons.adfgvxNotSet: Letters outside ADFGVX appear — not a fractionated ADFGVX transmission.
reasons.nihilistDigits: {{pairs}} digit pairs in the classic Nihilist sum range (22–110).
reasons.homophonicFlat: {{symbols}} distinct symbols — more than any single-letter substitution alphabet holds.
reasons.knownText.saknussemm: This is the Arne Saknussemm parchment from Jules Verne's “Journey to the Centre of the Earth” — {{letters}} matching letters.

letters.label: Letters
letters.hint: Letters extracted from the input — digits, punctuation and spaces are stripped before analysis.

ic.label: Index of coincidence
ic.hint: The chance that two random letters of the text are identical. English sits near 0.067, random letters near 0.038; noticeably lower values point to polyalphabetic ciphers.

directChi.label: Direct fit
directChi.hint: How English the letter frequencies are as the text stands, 0–100. High with a low sorted fit means the letters were moved, not replaced.

sortedChi.label: Sorted fit
sortedChi.hint: How English the frequency shape is once both sides are sorted, 0–100. Stays high under any monoalphabetic substitution.

caesar.label: Best shift
caesar.hint: The Caesar shift that makes the text most English, with its score. A wide gap to the runner-up means a plain shift cipher.

period.label: Best period
period.hint: The most likely repeating key length, with the index of coincidence of the slices at that period.

distinct.label: Distinct letters
distinct.hint: How many different letters appear. Playfair never emits J and uses at most 25 letters.

digitPairs.label: Digit pairs
digitPairs.hint: Two-digit groups in the input (total and distinct) — the output shape of Polybius-based ciphers such as Nihilist.

symbols.label: Distinct symbols
symbols.hint: All distinct characters in the input. Homophonic substitution uses more symbols than the alphabet has letters.

tooltips.multiplierCards: All twelve valid multipliers, ranked by how English the best shift for each looks. Pick one, adjust the shift on the next step.

wizard.assumption: The discs are the tool’s fixed ones, so the unknowns are the period and the disc step. Exact for ciphertexts whose plaintext letters all sit on the disc (like the practice challenges) — dropped letters shift the chunks otherwise.

tooltips.periodCards: Chunk sizes ranked by how English the best disc step for each decrypts. Pick one; the disc step comes next.
tooltips.stepCards: Disc turns ranked by English-likeness for the chosen period. The live preview confirms the choice.

settings.alphabetHint: Top row: plain alphabet. Bottom row: the cipher alphabet it maps to.

freeAlphabetError.empty: Type an alphabet first — all 26 letters, in any order.
freeAlphabetError.length: An alphabet needs exactly 26 letters — this one has a different count (spaces and punctuation are ignored).
freeAlphabetError.duplicates: Every letter may appear only once — this alphabet repeats a letter.

count.summary: {{letters}} letters, {{distinct}} distinct symbols, sorted by frequency.
count.hint: Compare the bars with English: the tallest cells should be E, T, A, O… Reading the shape first makes every later guess cheaper.

obvious.hint: Click a glowing cell, then pick the plaintext letter you think it stands for. The suggestion under a cell is only a hint — the decision is yours. The partial text below updates after every click.

words.hint: With a few letters placed, whole words become readable. A candidate in green fits the letters you already assigned — click it to place it.
words.none: No word patterns fit yet — go back and assign a few more letters, or continue to the gaps.
words.apply: Place this word: assigns a letter to every symbol of the cipher word.
words.doubles: Doubled letters in the ciphertext ({{doubles}}) — in English usually LL, TT, SS, EE or OO.
words.oneLetter: One-letter words ({{words}}) — in English only A and I.

gaps.hint: Fill the remaining cells. Watch the partial text: where a guess reads wrong, undo it and try the runner-up.

done.alphabet: Recovered cipher alphabet (plain A → Z on top, cipher letter below):
done.noKeyword: The alphabet is not keyword-shaped — a mixed alphabet was used.
done.incomplete: Assign every symbol of the ciphertext to unlock "Use this key".
done.fillNote: Plain letters that never appear in the text keep their default fill — they cannot be recovered from this text.

tooltips.suggestions: Ranks each unassigned symbol over the English frequency order. A hint only — nothing is assigned without your click.
tooltips.patterns: Cipher words whose shape matches a common English word (THE, AND…), consistent with your assignments. Clicking a candidate places the word.
tooltips.doubles: Doubled letters and one-letter words are strong clues in English.

settings.gridHint: The text written row-wise; the badges give the column reading order.

width.hint: The ciphertext was cut into columns and stacked. Its length must divide evenly by the column count — pick a candidate; the match score says how English-like the best column arrangement looks.

order.hint: Drag the column strips (or select one and use ‹ ›) until the rows read like English. The badges score each neighbouring pair; a wrong order still shows all the right letters.
order.bestPartner: The outlined column ({{position}}) reads best after the selected one — try moving it next.

done.hint: This is the recovered plaintext (padding letters may trail at the end). Use this result to decrypt with the same column order in the Tool tab.

tooltips.badges: How English-like two neighbouring columns look together. High numbers in green — low ones mean the pair is probably wrong.
tooltips.bestPartner: Outlines the column that scores best after the selected one. A hint only — the move is yours.
tooltips.livePreview: The plaintext the current column order produces, updating as you drag.

repeats.title: Repeated sequences
repeats.none: No repeated sequences found. Use the key length cards below instead.

keyLetters.allLocked: All letters set. Continue to step 3.
keyLetters.keyHint: Type a letter to override, clear it to un-lock.

cribs.title: Cribs
cribs.inputLabel: Word you think is in the message
cribs.noMatches: The word does not fit anywhere with this key length.

reason.kasiski-and-ic: {{count}} repeat gaps divisible by this length, slices look like English (IC {{ic}})
reason.kasiski-only: {{count}} repeat gaps divisible by this length
reason.weak: no strong evidence for this length

tooltips.key: The secret key. Every letter of the message is shifted by the matching key letter; the key repeats over the whole message.
tooltips.alphabet: The set of letters the cipher works with. Paste any letters — the tool uppercases them and drops duplicates. The default is the English alphabet.
tooltips.unknownKey: Check this if you do not know the key. A guided cracker opens below: it helps you find the key length and then every key letter, step by step.

toggle.highlightRepeats: Colours repeated letter groups in the text — the distances between them hint at the key length.
toggle.showGaps: Shows the distances between repeated sequences, next to each group.

tooltips.keyLengthCards: Likely key lengths ranked by two signals: distances between repeated sequences, and how English-like the text slices look. Click a card to choose.
tooltips.otherLength: Enter a key length manually if none of the suggested cards fits.
tooltips.sliceTabs: With a key length of N the text splits into N slices; every letter of a slice is shifted by the same key letter. Click a tab to work on that slice.
tooltips.keyStrip: Your key as you build it. Click a cell to jump to its slice, type a letter to override the chart choice, clear a cell to un-set it.
tooltips.cribInput: If you guess a word that appears in the plaintext, the cracker computes which key letters it implies, at every position it fits.
tooltips.apply: Fill the empty key slots with the letters this position suggests. Letters already set differently are never overwritten.

cracker.alphabetUnsupported: The frequency tables behind the cracker are English — switch the alphabet back to the standard 26 letters to use it.

improve.noImprovement: No single swap improves the score anymore — the square is as good as hill-climbing gets it. Try a manual swap or a new start.
improve.swapHint: Click two cells to swap them by hand — every manual swap is reversible.

done.keyLabel: Recovered key (read the square row by row):

tooltips.startKeyword: A keyword you suspect is in the square. Optional — random squares work too.
tooltips.improve: Try every cell swap and keep the single best one. Watch the preview: you stop when it reads like English.
tooltips.auto: Repeat improve-steps until nothing improves. Slower to undo by hand, but every pass stays visible in the preview.

columns.hint: The ciphertext is K equal chunks, one per transposition column, read in key order. Arrange the chunks into the grid slots: click two chips to swap them. Swapping the two chips of one pair flips that pair.

tooltips.keyLengthCards: Candidate column counts, ranked by how strongly the columns tie together. A hint, not a verdict — try another if the preview stays garbage.
tooltips.otherLength: Try any column count from 4 to 12.
tooltips.autoSuggest: Refill the arrangement with the strongest pairing the statistics find.

toggle.autoSuggest: Offer the statistically best column arrangement as a starting point.

tooltips.assignLetter: Pick the plaintext letter for this symbol, or clear it.
tooltips.cribInput: A word you expect in the message. Matches respect the letters you already assigned.
tooltips.symbolChart: The symbols of the ciphertext once the columns are arranged. Click a symbol to assign its plaintext letter; the count shows how often it appears.

tooltips.hintPresets: How much help the tool gives: Easy shows everything, Hard leaves the thinking to you.
tooltips.undo: Take the last assignment back — nothing breaks.
tooltips.redo: Re-apply the assignment you just undid.
tooltips.chartArrows: Rotate the chart with the buttons or the arrow keys; the rotation is the key letter.
tooltips.matchScore: How English-like the current rotation looks (chi-squared score).
tooltips.skip: Leave the cracker without using anything.
tooltips.useThisKey: Fill the key fields with the recovered key.

toggle.confidenceBars: Show how strong each candidate is.
toggle.englishReference: Show the English frequency reference next to the observed bars.
toggle.livePreview: Show the partially decrypted message as you work.
toggle.cribs: Search for a probable word (crib) and apply its letters at once.

wizard.inputChanged: The ciphertext changed — the analysis restarted.

warnings.shortText: Short texts crack unreliably — 100+ letters give dependable results.
warnings.shortSlice: Fewer than 20 letters in this slice — treat the suggestion with suspicion.

assignment.clickCell: Click a cell, then pick the plaintext letter you think it stands for.
assignment.conflict: {{letter}} is assigned to more than one symbol — a substitution maps each cipher symbol to exactly one letter.

grid.moveLeft: Move this column one step left
grid.moveRight: Move this column one step right

vigenere.description: Each letter of the message is shifted by the matching letter of a repeating key.
vigenere.origin: Described by Giovan Battista Bellaso in 1553, later misattributed to Blaise de Vigenère.

controls.rotate-left: the left arrow under the discs
controls.rotate-right: the right arrow under the discs
controls.grid-toggle: the "Leave the last row incomplete" checkbox

vigenere.1467: Leon Battista Alberti invents the cipher disk — the first idea of using several alphabets.
vigenere.1508: Johannes Trithemius publishes the tabula recta, a table of all letter shifts.
vigenere.1553: Giovan Battista Bellaso describes the repeating-key cipher with an easy-to-remember key phrase.
vigenere.1586: Blaise de Vigenère publishes a similar cipher; the repeating-key scheme is later misattributed to him.
vigenere.1863: Friedrich Kasiski publishes a general method for finding the key length (Charles Babbage had broken it privately a decade earlier).
vigenere.1920s: William Friedman develops the index of coincidence, making the attack statistical and rigorous.

keyword.800: Al-Kindi writes on decrypting messages by letter frequency in Baghdad — the standing verdict on every fixed substitution cipher, keyword alphabets included.
keyword.1563: Giambattista della Porta's De Furtivis Literarum Notis puts keyed alphabets into the cipher manuals: the keyword's letters first, the remainder after.
keyword.1586: The Babington correspondence — a fixed substitution at its core — is read by Thomas Phelippes' frequency analysis; Mary, Queen of Scots is executed on the evidence.

columnar.wwi: Columnar transposition — usually doubled — is a standard field cipher of several First World War armies.
columnar.1918: ADFGVX chains fractionation with a keyed columnar transposition; Painvin has to undo the column order first.
columnar.1942: SOE agents behind enemy lines use double transposition keyed by memorised poems — Leo Marks' verse keys.

caesar.121: Suetonius describes both Caesar's shift of 3 and Augustus' shift of 1 in The Lives of the Twelve Caesars.
caesar.800: Al-Kindi writes on decrypting messages by letter frequency, breaking every single-alphabet substitution cipher.
caesar.1553: Bellaso's repeating-key cipher — "many Caesars", one per key letter — makes fixed shifts obsolete.
caesar.58bc: Julius Caesar uses a shift of 3 for private correspondence, his biographer Suetonius reports.

alberti.1467: Leon Battista Alberti presents the cipher disk in De Cifris — the first idea of using several alphabets.
alberti.1508: Johannes Trithemius publishes the tabula recta, a square table of all alphabets, extending the disk idea.
alberti.1553: Giovan Battista Bellaso turns the alphabets with a repeating key phrase — the scheme later called the Vigenère cipher.

affine.850: Al-Kindi's frequency analysis dooms every single-alphabet cipher, affine rules included.
affine.1976: Diffie and Hellman introduce public-key cryptography, making modular arithmetic the backbone of modern ciphers.
affine.58bc: Julius Caesar's shift cipher — the Affine cipher's a = 1 special case — protects his military messages.

atbash.1100: Medieval commentators (Rashi, then Radak) discuss the Atbash passages of Jeremiah, the oldest attested substitution cipher.
atbash.586bc: The Book of Jeremiah writes Babylon as SHESHACH and the Chaldeans as LEV-KAMAI — Atbash readings confirmed by commentators.

morse.1837: Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail develop the electric telegraph and the first version of their code.
morse.1844: Morse taps "What hath God wrought" over the Washington–Baltimore line, the first official telegraph message.
morse.1865: The Paris telegraph convention adopts Gerke's revision as International Morse — the code used today.
morse.1906: The Berlin radiotelegraph convention adopts SOS as the worldwide maritime distress signal.
morse.1999: The Global Maritime Distress and Safety System ends Morse's official watch at sea.

base64.1992: MIME introduces base64 so email can carry attachments over text-only channels.
base64.1996: RFC 2045 fixes the exact 64-character alphabet that email still uses.
base64.2006: RFC 4648 consolidates the base encodings, including the URL-safe variant.

rot13.1980s: Usenet's net.jokes newsgroup adopts ROT13 to hide spoilers and punchlines; it becomes netiquette.

playfair.1854: Charles Wheatstone invents the digraph cipher; Lord Playfair promotes it to the British establishment.
playfair.1899: British forces use the Playfair cipher for tactical messages in the Second Boer War.
playfair.1914: The First World War's large wireless traffic feeds digraph frequency analysis, and the cipher loses its edge.

enigma.1918: Arthur Scherbius patents the Enigma in Germany; the commercial machine follows in 1923.
enigma.1926: The German Navy adopts the Enigma; the Army follows in 1928 — the Wehrmacht's confidence grows into doctrine.
enigma.1932: Marian Rejewski of the Polish Cipher Bureau reconstructs the Enigma wiring mathematically, using the doubled message key.
enigma.1939: At the Pyry conference the Poles hand the British and French their Enigma methods, replicas and the bomba — weeks before the war.
enigma.1940: The first British bombe, Victory, starts work at Bletchley Park against the daily traffic.
enigma.1942: The U-boats move to the four-rotor M4 ('Shark'); Atlantic decrypts go dark for about ten months.

adfgvx.1918-introduced: Fritz Nebel’s fractionation-transposition cipher enters German field service as ADFGX, with a 5×5 square.
adfgvx.1918-painvin: Georges Painvin breaks the ADFGX traffic from intercepted same-key message pairs after months of effort.
adfgvx.1918-traffic: The square gains a sixth row for digits (ADFGVX); the broken traffic helps the French anticipate the German offensive at Amiens.

pigpen.1531: Cornelius Agrippa describes an early Rosicrucian-style grid cipher — the 'Kabbalah of the Nine Chambers', dots carrying the alphabet.
pigpen.1730: The pirate Olivier Levasseur allegedly throws a pigpen scrap into the crowd at his execution — the unread treasure note dies with its variant.
pigpen.1700s: Freemasons adopt the cipher for lodge records and correspondence — so persistently that it becomes 'the Freemason's cipher'.
pigpen.1860s: Union prisoners in Confederate prisons use pigpen to smuggle messages during the American Civil War.

vigenere-easy-1.title: Break a message from the novel
vigenere-easy-1.hint2: The key is a common pet: three letters.

vigenere-easy-2.title: The novel continues
vigenere-easy-2.hint2: The key is a citrus fruit.

vigenere-medium-1.title: A truth universally acknowledged
vigenere-medium-1.hint2: The key is a fruit again — six letters this time.

vigenere-medium-2.title: Once upon a midnight dreary
vigenere-medium-2.hint2: The key names the bird of the poem.

vigenere-hard-1.title: To be or not to be
vigenere-hard-1.hint1: The key length is 11 — frequency hints get shaky, a crib is safer.
vigenere-hard-1.hint2: The key is a songbird that sings at night.
vigenere-hard-1.hint3: The word TOBE appears at the very start — place it as a crib.

vigenere-hard-2.title: Four score and seven
vigenere-hard-2.hint1: The key length is 10 — use a crib.
vigenere-hard-2.hint2: The key is an adjective meaning impossible to decode.
vigenere-hard-2.hint3: The opening FOURSCORE works as a crib.

caesar-easy-1.title: Fear itself
caesar-easy-1.hint1: The shift is the classic one — the number Caesar himself used.
caesar-easy-1.hint2: The shift is 3: THE becomes WKH.

caesar-medium-1.title: Eliminate the impossible
caesar-medium-1.hint1: Frequency analysis: the most frequent ciphertext letter is the encrypted E.
caesar-medium-1.hint2: The shift is 11 — count the letters: E becomes P.

caesar-hard-1.title: Friends, Romans, countrymen
caesar-hard-1.hint1: The shift is 23 — small enough to walk through by hand.
caesar-hard-1.hint2: The ciphertext hides the start of a famous Roman speech.

alberti-easy-1.title: I came, I saw, I conquered
alberti-easy-1.hint1: The disc turns after every 2 letters — the period is 2.
alberti-easy-1.hint2: The step is 3, and the discs start at their default alignment; reload the page if you turned them.

alberti-medium-1.title: Per aspera ad astra
alberti-medium-1.hint2: The step is 4 — after every chunk the inner disc jumps four positions.

alberti-hard-1.title: All Gaul
alberti-hard-1.hint3: It is the opening of Julius Caesar's Gallic War — written with the 20 letters of Alberti's disc only.

affine-demo.title: Known-plaintext demo ciphertext
affine-demo.hint1: You know the message starts with ATTACK. See what A and T encrypt to, then solve the line y = a·x + b.

affine-easy-1.title: Fortune favors the brave
affine-easy-1.hint1: The multiplier is 3 and the shift is 7 — encrypting A gives H.
affine-easy-1.hint2: Check yourself: S should encrypt to J.

affine-medium-1.title: Elementary
affine-medium-1.hint1: You recognise the opening: the plaintext starts with THE — and T encrypts to O while E encrypts to N.
affine-medium-1.hint2: Two pairs give the line: y₁ − y₂ ≡ a·(x₁ − x₂) (mod 26). Find a, then b.

affine-hard-1.title: Fourscore and seven
affine-hard-1.hint1: It is the opening of a famous American speech.
affine-hard-1.hint2: You intercept two pairs: F encrypts to I, and O encrypts to D.
affine-hard-1.hint3: Solve a from the two pairs (you need a modular inverse), then b from either pair.

atbash-easy-1.title: Keep this secret
atbash-easy-1.hint1: There is no key: Atbash has exactly one fixed mapping. Switch to decrypt mode and paste the cryptogram.
atbash-easy-1.hint2: In Atbash, A becomes Z, B becomes Y — the alphabet read backwards.

atbash-medium-1.title: In God we trust
atbash-medium-1.hint1: Atbash is its own inverse: encrypting and decrypting are the same operation.
atbash-medium-1.hint2: The mapping is public — no search needed, just apply the mirror.

atbash-hard-1.title: Fourscore and seven
atbash-hard-1.hint1: It opens a famous American speech.
atbash-hard-1.hint2: No key to find: the whole secret is the fixed mirror A↔Z.

keyword-demo.title: Cracker demo ciphertext
keyword-demo.hint1: The spaces survive encryption — word shapes are your friend. The word that keeps appearing is probably THE.

columnar-demo.title: Warm-up: the road north
columnar-demo.hint1: The ciphertext is 56 letters — its divisors include 4. Four columns fit the grid; start there.

keyword-easy-1.title: The best of times
keyword-easy-1.hint1: The keyword has six letters, all different.
keyword-easy-1.hint2: The most frequent symbol is almost surely the encrypted E — assign it first and watch the text wake up.

columnar-easy-1.title: Four columns of Dickens
columnar-easy-1.hint1: The true width divides the padded length evenly — and 4 is a strong candidate. Rank, pick, then drag.
columnar-easy-1.hint2: Two neighbouring columns form real digraphs (TH, HE, IN) when zipped row by row — watch the green badges.

keyword-medium-1.title: A truth universally acknowledged
keyword-medium-1.hint1: The keyword has seven letters, no repeats.
keyword-medium-1.hint2: The opening words are famous — IT and IS are one-letter-away once T and I are placed.

columnar-medium-1.title: Six columns of Austen
columnar-medium-1.hint1: Six columns. Find the pair with the highest badge score — they are true neighbours in the grid.
columnar-medium-1.hint2: Build the chain from the best pair outward: every column has exactly one neighbour on each side.

keyword-hard-1.title: Four score and seven
keyword-hard-1.hint2: FOUR SCORE opens the message — the word shapes do most of the work once F, O, U, R are placed.

columnar-hard-1.title: Seven columns from Gettysburg
columnar-hard-1.hint1: Seven columns. The best-partner outline (Easy preset) is gone at this difficulty — rely on the badges.
columnar-hard-1.hint2: Famous opening lines are cribs: slide FOURSCORE against candidate column pairs in your head.

morse-easy-1.title: The eagle has landed
morse-easy-1.hint1: Letters are separated by single spaces, words by a slash.
morse-easy-1.hint2: Switch the tool to decrypt mode and paste the code as it is.

morse-medium-1.title: What hath God wrought
morse-medium-1.hint1: The message is the first official telegraph transmission, from Washington to Baltimore in 1844.
morse-medium-1.hint2: In the tool, a space between letters stays a space; the word gaps are slashes.

morse-hard-1.title: Struck an iceberg
morse-hard-1.hint1: A paraphrase of the distress traffic from a famous ship in April 1912.
morse-hard-1.hint2: Spacing is everything: check that no space was lost when copying.
morse-hard-1.hint3: The message begins with the distress signal itself — three dots, three dashes, three dots.

base64-easy-1.title: Meet me at dawn
base64-easy-1.hint1: This is an encoding, not a cipher — no key exists. Switch the tool to decrypt mode and paste.
base64-easy-1.hint2: The alphabet is A–Z a–z 0–9 + /, with = padding the tail.

base64-medium-1.title: All that glisters
base64-medium-1.hint1: A line from Shakespeare — paste the string into decrypt mode.
base64-medium-1.hint2: The single = at the end is padding: the last chunk carried two bytes.

base64-hard-1.title: Eliminate the impossible
base64-hard-1.hint1: It is a Sherlock Holmes quotation — decode with the tool.
base64-hard-1.hint2: Letters-only comparison: the answer ignores spacing and case.

rot13-easy-1.title: The cake is a lie
rot13-easy-1.hint1: ROT13 is its own inverse — decoding is the very same operation.
rot13-easy-1.hint2: The shift is fixed at 13; there is no key to find.

rot13-medium-1.title: The punchline
rot13-medium-1.hint1: A legendary joke is traditionally told with its punchline posted separately — often in ROT13.
rot13-medium-1.hint2: Paste the text into decrypt mode; the tool does the half-turn for you.

rot13-hard-1.title: Two roads
rot13-hard-1.hint1: It is the opening image of a famous Robert Frost poem.
rot13-hard-1.hint2: Again there is no key: only the fixed 13-step rotation.
rot13-hard-1.hint3: Spacing is preserved, so word lengths are readable hints.

playfair-demo.title: Crib demo ciphertext
playfair-demo.hint1: A crib to start from: the message begins with ATTACK.

playfair-easy-1.title: Sailboat at dawn
playfair-easy-1.hint2: The tool folds J into I and pads doubled letters and odd tails with X.

playfair-medium-1.title: The game is afoot
playfair-medium-1.hint2: A famous Sherlock Holmes phrase about a game.

playfair-hard-1.title: The worst of times
playfair-hard-1.hint2: Dickens opens A Tale of Two Cities twice — this is the second half.
playfair-hard-1.hint3: Decrypt pairs with the tool; the plaintext has no doubled pairs, so no filler X appears.

enigma-demo.title: Crib and captured key
enigma-demo.hint1: The captured key sheet says the start positions were QCV — and the message begins with ATTACK. Set the key, paste, and read.

enigma-easy-1.title: Fair weather
enigma-easy-1.hint1: The key sheet for the day says: start positions AAA.
enigma-easy-1.hint2: Type the ciphertext into decrypt mode; the machine does the rest.

enigma-medium-1.title: Reinforcements at dawn
enigma-medium-1.hint2: A military report about the morning's movements.

enigma-hard-1.title: The obvious fact
enigma-hard-1.hint2: A Sherlock Holmes maxim about deception.
enigma-hard-1.hint3: Only letters travel — the answer is the plaintext without spaces.

adfgvx-demo.title: Order of the day
adfgvx-demo.hint1: Both keys are known: square NIGHT, transposition GERMAN, ADFGVX variant. Open the cracker to see how the tool would have found them.

adfgvx-easy-1.title: Final resting place
adfgvx-easy-1.hint1: The variant is ADFGVX and the square key is NIGHT.
adfgvx-easy-1.hint2: The transposition key is GERMAN — six distinct letters.
adfgvx-easy-1.hint3: Type both keys into the tool and decrypt.

adfgvx-medium-1.title: A tale of two eras
adfgvx-medium-1.hint1: The transposition key is WINTER. Its length gives you the column count.
adfgvx-medium-1.hint2: With the columns ordered, the symbols are a plain substitution — use the frequency suggestions.
adfgvx-medium-1.hint3: The square key is NIGHT if you want to check yourself.

adfgvx-hard-1.title: Dedication
adfgvx-hard-1.hint1: The variant is ADFGVX and the transposition key has six distinct letters.
adfgvx-hard-1.hint2: A crib: the message starts with the word WE.

pigpen-easy-1.title: The buried map
pigpen-easy-1.hint1: Count the shapes: full boxes, corners and open pens — the walls tell you which pen of the grid a letter lived in.
pigpen-easy-1.hint2: Dotted pens come after plain ones: A–I are undotted, J–R dotted. The legend in the tool is the key.

pigpen-medium-1.title: To be or not to be
pigpen-medium-1.hint1: Longer text is easier: the most frequent glyph is almost surely E, T or A.
pigpen-medium-1.hint2: Doubled glyphs are L, T or E — the classic doubles of English.

pigpen-hard-1.title: A tale of two cities
pigpen-hard-1.hint1: This is still a fixed substitution: identify a few high-frequency glyphs first and the rest follows.
pigpen-hard-1.hint2: Look for the pattern IT…AS…TH… — opening phrases of famous novels give strong cribs.
pigpen-hard-1.hint3: The variant is the classic masonic key; the legend in the tool lists every mapping.

pigpen.variant: The symbol set: the same cipher drawn with different grids and marks — the reader must know the variant.
pigpen.key: Add this glyph to the message.

tooltips.swap: Swaps the two sides: the tool flips between encrypting and decrypting. The current mode shows in the header.
tooltips.alphabet: The alphabet the cipher works with: pick a preset or paste your own ordered letters.

caesar.rotation: The shift: every letter of the message advances by this many positions in the alphabet (backwards in decrypt mode).
caesar.keepSpaces: Keep spaces: preserves the layout of words instead of removing them all.
caesar.keepCase: Keep case: preserves capitals instead of writing everything in capitals.

affine.multiplier: The multiplier a of y = a·x + b. It must be coprime with the alphabet length, or several letters collide.
affine.shift: The shift b of y = a·x + b — the Caesar-like addition applied after the multiplication.

alberti.disc: Alberti's cipher disc: the fixed outer ring carries the plaintext alphabet, the movable inner ring the mixed cipher alphabet.
alberti.increment: The rotation step: how many positions the inner disc jumps after each period.
alberti.period: The period: how many letters are encrypted before the inner disc turns.

keyword.keyword: The keyword builds the cipher alphabet: its letters first (duplicates dropped), then the remaining letters in order.
keyword.continueFromLast: Instead of continuing from A after the keyword, keep counting from the keyword's last letter.
keyword.freeAlphabet: Skip the keyword and type any arrangement of all 26 letters — every letter exactly once.
keyword.keepSpaces: Keep spaces: preserves the layout of words instead of removing them all.
keyword.keepCase: Keep case: preserves capitals instead of writing everything in capitals.

columnar.keyword: The keyword fixes the column order: its letters sorted alphabetically say which column is read first, second, third…
columnar.secondKeyword: A second keyword transposes the already-transposed text — the classic double transposition.
columnar.double: Double transposition: encrypt with the first keyword, then transposition the result again with the second.
columnar.irregular: Leave the last row incomplete: no padding letter is added, so the last row stays short (the classic hand cipher).
columnar.keepSpaces: Keep spaces: spaces ride the zigzag like letters instead of being stripped.

atbash.alphabet: The alphabet selector: Atbash mirrors the chosen alphabet — the only choice the cipher offers.

morse.dot: The character playing the short signal (the dot) in the encoded output.
morse.dash: The character playing the long signal (the dash) in the encoded output.

tooltips.playfair.key: The keyword: once deduplicated it seeds the 5×5 letter square — the cipher's entire key.
tooltips.enigma.key: The rotors' start positions (the Grundstellung) — three letters A–Z. On the real machine, the key also carried the rotor order, the ring settings and the plugboard pairs.

adfgvx.variant: The variant: ADFGX uses a 5×5 letter square, ADFGVX adds a sixth row with the digits 0–9.
adfgvx.square-key: The keyed square: the key's letters fill the square first (duplicates removed, J folded into I), the rest of the alphabet follows. Change it and both the coordinates and the final transposition change.
adfgvx.transposition-key: The transposition key: its letters fix the number and reading order of the columns that shuffle the fractionated text.
adfgvx.unknown-keys: Check this when you don't know the keys: a guided cracker opens below and walks you from the ciphertext to both keys.

caesar.description: Every letter of the message is shifted by the same fixed number of positions in the alphabet.
caesar.origin: Named after Julius Caesar, who reportedly used a shift of 3 in private correspondence.

alberti.description: The first polyalphabetic cipher: two rotating discs switch alphabets every few letters.
alberti.origin: Devised by Leon Battista Alberti around 1467 on his cipher disk, Formula.

affine.description: A substitution driven by the line y = a·x + b: multiply the letter, then shift, all mod 26.
affine.origin: A mathematical generalisation of the Caesar shift, named after the affine function ax + b.

atbash.description: The mirror cipher: the alphabet is flipped over, so A becomes Z and B becomes Y. No key at all.
atbash.origin: Hebrew scribes; attested in the Book of Jeremiah.

keyword.description: A substitution whose cipher alphabet is spelled out by a keyword: its letters first, then the rest in order.
keyword.origin: A classic keyed alphabet, described in early cryptologic manuals; popular with hobbyists ever since.

columnar.origin: Field ciphers; made famous by ADFGVX and the SOE

morse.description: An encoding, not a cipher: every letter becomes a public pattern of dots and dashes for the telegraph.
morse.origin: Developed by Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail for the electric telegraph (1830s–1840s).

base64.description: An encoding, not a cipher: three bytes become four characters from a fixed 64-symbol alphabet.
base64.origin: Standardised for MIME email attachments (Nathaniel Borenstein, RFC 2045).

rot13.description: A fixed shift of 13 — its own inverse: applying it twice restores the text. Obfuscation, not encryption.
rot13.origin: Popularised on Usenet newsgroups to hide spoilers and punchlines.

playfair.description: A digraph cipher: letter pairs move over a 5×5 square built from a keyword — the same letter encrypts differently depending on its partner.
playfair.origin: Invented by Charles Wheatstone in 1854 and championed by Lord Playfair.

enigma.description: A rotor machine: three wheels and a reflector reshuffle the alphabet with every keypress.
enigma.origin: Invented by Arthur Scherbius in Germany; patented 1918, adopted by the German military from 1926.

adfgvx.description: The German WWI field cipher that split every letter into two of six letters and then shuffled the result — until Georges Painvin broke it.
adfgvx.origin: Fritz Nebel, German army signal corps

pigpen.description: A symbol substitution: every letter becomes a fragment of a grid — the famous Freemason's cipher.
pigpen.origin: Popularly the Freemasons, who used it for records and rites; earlier variants are older still.

plaintext.name: Plaintext
plaintext.definition: The original readable message before encryption.

ciphertext.name: Ciphertext
ciphertext.definition: The scrambled message produced by encryption.

cryptogram.name: Cryptogram
cryptogram.definition: A message written in cipher; on this site it also names the input field.

key.name: Key
key.definition: The secret that controls how the text is scrambled.

alphabet.name: Alphabet
alphabet.definition: The set of letters the cipher works with.

key-length.name: Key length
key-length.definition: How many letters the key has before it starts repeating.

shift.name: Shift
shift.definition: How far a letter moves along the alphabet.

substitution.name: Substitution
substitution.definition: Replacing each letter with another one.

cipher-alphabet.name: Cipher alphabet
cipher-alphabet.definition: The reordered alphabet a substitution maps the plain alphabet onto — in this cipher, spelled out by the keyword.

pattern-word.name: Pattern word
pattern-word.definition: A word recognised by the shape of its repeated letters: THE has the pattern ABC, THAT ABCA — the shape survives any substitution.

polyalphabetic.name: Polyalphabetic
polyalphabetic.definition: A cipher that uses several alphabets in turn instead of one.

slice.name: Slice
slice.definition: Every Nth letter of the text (N = key length). All letters of one slice are shifted by the same key letter.

frequency-analysis.name: Frequency analysis
frequency-analysis.definition: Studying how often letters appear; comparing the counts with the language reveals the plaintext.

index-of-coincidence.name: Index of coincidence
index-of-coincidence.definition: A number (about 0.067 for English) showing how likely two random letters of a text are equal.

kasiski-examination.name: Kasiski examination
kasiski-examination.definition: Finding the key length from the distances between repeated sequences in the ciphertext.

crib.name: Crib
crib.definition: A word you guess is in the plaintext; comparing it with the ciphertext reveals key letters.

brute-force.name: Brute force
brute-force.definition: Trying every possible key until the message makes sense; possible only when the key space is small.

period.name: Period
period.definition: How many letters are encrypted before the disc or alphabet changes; after each period the substitution starts over.

modular-arithmetic.name: Modular arithmetic
modular-arithmetic.definition: Counting that wraps around at a fixed size: after the maximum you start again at zero, like hours on a clock.

encoding.name: Encoding
encoding.definition: A reversible rewrite of data for transport or storage; anyone can undo it, so it hides nothing.

dot.name: Dot
dot.definition: Morse's short signal — one unit of sound, light or current.

dash.name: Dash
dash.definition: Morse's long signal — three units long, with pauses of one unit between the symbols of a letter.

digraph.name: Digraph
digraph.definition: A pair of letters treated as a single unit; Playfair encrypts digraphs, not single letters.

rotor.name: Rotor
rotor.definition: A wired wheel that maps letters through a fixed scrambling and rotates one step per keypress, changing the mapping as you type.

plugboard.name: Plugboard
plugboard.definition: A panel of cable pairs swapping letters before and after the rotors; the main multiplier of Enigma's key space.

reflector.name: Reflector
reflector.definition: A fixed, self-inverse wiring that bounces the signal back through the rotors; it makes Enigma reciprocal but never maps a letter to itself.

polybius-square.name: Polybius square
polybius-square.definition: A grid that turns each character into two coordinates: the row and the column of its cell.

fractionation.name: Fractionation
fractionation.definition: Splitting each plaintext letter into several smaller units (here: two coordinates) before the next cipher layer.

transposition.name: Transposition
transposition.definition: Changing the order of symbols without changing the symbols themselves.

column-order.name: Column order
column-order.definition: The order in which the columns of a transposition grid are read out — fixed by the keyword: its letters sorted alphabetically say which column comes first.

anagramming.name: Anagramming
anagramming.definition: Rebuilding a transposed text by sliding column fragments side by side until rows read like the language — the classic hand attack on transposition ciphers.
